abstract.p: Genetic interactions can reveal gene function and identify cancer-relevant synthetic lethals, but systematic mapping in human cells is constrained by inefficient reagents, vast combinatorial search space, and diversity of cell types. Here, we leverage principles from yeast genetic networks to identify human gene modules enriched for genetic interactions. Using our Cas12a-based In4mer combinatorial knockout platform, we screen all pairwise interactions within receptor tyrosine kinase and DNA damage response modules across eight diverse cancer cell lines. We identify hundreds of unreported synthetic lethals, including a dense network within the protein glycosylation machinery, and confirm that interactions in 2D cell culture are maintained in more physiologically relevant models. Our targeted modules show up to 16-fold enrichment of interaction density, providing a scalable strategy for systematic interaction mapping.

body.p: Genetic interactions provide a fundamental framework for deciphering how genes work together to control the emergence of phenotype at the cellular and organismal level. Genetic interaction occurs when the combined effect of perturbing two genes deviates from the expected effect from single perturbation(1, 2). Synthetic lethality, the limiting case of genetic interaction where double knockout causes cell death, has long offered a compelling paradigm for cancer(3), through an array of related but distinct exploits. For example, identification of vulnerabilities arising from tumor-specific genetic lesions grew from the discovery of PARP inhibitor sensitivity in BRCA-mutated cancers(4, 5), later expanding to include homologous recombination deficiency more broadly. More recently, tumors with defective mismatch repair machinery were discovered to be specifically sensitive to loss of Werner helicase (WRN)(6).

Extending this approach beyond tumor-specific lesions – to identify, e.g., independently druggable SL gene pairs with synergistic activity (Fig. 1A) – requires combinatorial perturbation approaches. In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, knockouts of over 23 million double mutants identified hundreds of thousands of quantitative genetic interactions yielding a global network that covers more than 90% of yeast genes(7, 8). This comprehensive network established several foundational principles: genes encoding proteins that function together in the same pathway or complex tend to share similar patterns of genetic interactions; these correlated genetic interaction profiles define functional modules corresponding to protein complexes, biological processes, and biochemical pathways; and genetic interactions are enriched within and between functionally related modules(9–11).

However, replicating GI networks established in yeast is considerably more challenging in human cells due to the larger genome, greater biological complexity, and cell-type heterogeneity. Genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screening across hundreds of cell lines paved the way for discovery of context-specific genetic vulnerabilities as well as the construction of co-essentiality networks(6, 12–15) that indicate functional relationships. Additionally, the development of combinatorial and multiplex perturbation technologies has enabled direct measurement of GI in human cells(16–28), but at high experimental cost. Large-scale screen efforts by Horlbeck et al.(22) and recently by Fielden et al.(19) used over 1 million and nearly 680,000 dual-guide Cas9 constructs, respectively. Though highly informative, these studies each assayed only ~0.1% of the possible search space in one or two cell lines, highlighting the resource-intensive and technically challenging limitations of combinatorial screening in mammalian cells. Considering the cost, scale and limited reproducibility of large-scale screens, some studies have focused on exploration of paralogs(29–31), which often exhibit functional redundancy and are more enriched for SL. Together, these limitations highlight the need for improved multiplex technologies and predictive models that prioritize genes with high interaction potential.

Here, we leverage principles from the yeast genetic interaction network to predict which regions of the human genome are likely to be enriched for genetic interactions and test the top predictions with our CRISPR/Cas12a In4mer platform. In4mer uses the RNA-processing capability of the Cas12a CRISPR endonuclease to process multiple guide RNAs expressed from a single transcript, enabling simultaneous targeting of multiple genes, each with multiple guides(32, 33). We and others have shown that enCas12a shows comparable or better efficiency than Cas9 platforms for surveying GI(32, 34–36), while reducing the number of constructs required to assay GI by as much as five-fold(35). Our screens identify hundreds of synthetic lethal and suppressor interactions, including extensive interactions within the ER-localized protein glycosylation machinery, and demonstrate that interactions discovered in permissive 2D culture are maintained in more physiologically relevant environments including 3D organoid models and mouse xenografts. Comparison with a randomly selected gene set confirms that our module-based predictions yield substantial enrichment of genetic interactions, establishing a principled framework for prioritizing combinatorial perturbation experiments in human cells.

sec.title: Network-guided prediction of genetic interactions
sec.p: In yeast screens, correlated genetic interaction profiles imply co-functionality (Fig. 1B), giving rise to functional interaction networks that both predict gene function and identify modules of coherent biological activity. It has previously been observed that these functional modules tend to be enriched for genetic interactions between their constituent genes, both in yeast(9–11) and recently in human cells(27), and, conversely, that interactions between genes in unrelated modules are extremely rare(8). We built on this knowledge to develop a method for decomposition of functional interaction networks that would facilitate discovery of modules with high proportion of genetic interactions (fig. S1, A to E). We discovered that, for the yeast network, the combination of relatively large module size and high functional coherence within the module combine to nominate specific gene sets that were enriched for within-module genetic interactions (Fig. 1C). We then took human gene essentiality data from CRISPR screens in cancer cell lines(37, 38), constructed an optimized functional interaction network using methods we have described previously(39) (Fig. 1D), and decomposed the human network using the same principles. We identified five large modules with very high functional enrichment (Fig. 1E), three of which (mitochondria, ribosome, and keratin) are relatively homogeneous clusters with less biological variation. We therefore focused on the remaining two modules for further study: one containing receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) genes and their biogenesis factors, and another with DNA damage response (DDR) genes.

The RTK module (Fig. 1F) is characterized by RTK genes that show high variation in gene essentiality across DepMap cell lines, including EGFR, FGFR1, IGF1R, MET, and INSR. Our functional network decomposition approach includes “moonlighter” genes and modules that are connected to disparate other modules in a context-dependent manner; e.g. the GRB2/SOS1/PTPN11 signal transduction module is connected with both the EGFR and FGFR1 modules. Close paralogs of each gene are added to each module; e.g. SOS1 paralog SOS2 is added to the signal transduction module. Notably, this global RTK network includes functional submodules encoding ER-based protein glycosylation and ER-associated degradation, and FGFR1-associated heparin sulfate biosynthesis, all elements required for the proper posttranslational processing and trafficking of cell surface receptors(40, 41). However, this module did not contain the classical downstream signaling components such as the MAP kinase and PI3 kinase pathways, which we added manually (fig. S1F). The total RTK module expanded from 144 genes in the main cluster to 199 genes across all clusters that we predicted would be enriched for genetic interactions. Similarly, we manually added smaller DDR clusters to the large DDR module (fig. S1G), for a final set of 167 genes in our prediction set.

To test these predictions, we developed a CRISPR genetic interaction library based on our In4mer platform(35). In4mer is a Cas12a-based system that expresses arrays of four individually addressable guide RNA. Our library design includes two arrays targeting each single gene with four guides each, and two arrays targeting each gene pair with two guides targeting each gene (Fig. 1G). The single library targets all combinations of 199 genes in the RTK module, all combinations of 167 genes in the DDR module, as well as all 4,435 paralog pairs and 376 paralog triples from our prior catalog, along with controls, in a single pool of 85k sequences (Fig. 1H).

We screened 12 adherent carcinoma cell lines with the library and evaluated each for quality control (figs. S2 and S3). Separation of essential and nonessential genes ranged from excellent (PC9 cells, Fig. 1I) to moderate (A549 cells, Fig. 1J). Based on Cohen’s D statistics across the 12 cell lines, which showed a bimodal distribution of effect sizes (Fig. 1K), we selected the top eight for detailed analysis. To facilitate comparison across cell lines, we normalized each screen’s fold change to a Z score (Zfc) by fitting the main peak of the overall fold change distribution to a normal distribution (Fig. 1L). Clustering of selected marker genes or gene pairs using Zfc clearly differentiated the eight high-quality screens by their oncogenic driver genes (Fig. 1M). Notably, BRAFmut cells (A375, HT29) also show strong dependence on IGF1R while EGFR cells (MDA-MB-468 and PC9) show strong dependence on the GRB2/SOS1/PTPN11 module. KRASmut cells are generally independent of upstream signaling elements, though SW837 cells are dependent on both KRAS and EGFR signaling. Overall, these preliminary results indicate the CRISPR screens are working as designed and provide a high-resolution view of the genetic dependencies of each cell line.

sec.title: Strong, context-specific genetic interactions in the RTK module
sec.p: To decipher genetic interactions from combinatorial knockouts, we developed the Genetic interaction Regression Analysis of Pairwise Effects (GRAPE) algorithm (Fig. 2A). GRAPE builds a regression model with a binary predictor matrix and learns the single gene knockout phenotypes (beta coefficients) that best fit the observed double gene knockout data. Raw genetic interactions are then measured as the difference between observed and expected fold change and are converted to Z-scores using a sliding window to calculate local standard deviation. As an example, the observed fold changes for all pairwise knockouts for the PC9 cell line are compared with the fold changes expected from the sum of the beta coefficients for each gene pair (Fig. 2B). Raw genetic interaction scores as well as a local standard deviation are calculated (Fig. 2C), and Z scores of genetic interaction (Zgi, Fig. 2D) show synthetic lethal interactions among paralog pairs in the RTK and DDR libraries. Importantly, the GRAPE approach estimates single gene knockout phenotype from hundreds of observations across gene pairs, rather than just the two guide arrays targeting each single gene (Fig. 2E), improving estimates of expected double knockout phenotype.

Focusing first on the RTK module, we observed strong, background-specific genetic interactions between paralogs in the RTK/MAPK signal transduction pathway. Fold change of all ~200 gene pairs of either SOS1 or SOS2, paralogous guanine nucleotide exchange factors for RAS proteins, are distributed around the beta scores for single knockouts, but double knockout shows severe fitness phenotype (Zfc ~ −4), specifically in EGFR-dependent cells, but not in KRAS- or BRAF-mutant backgrounds (Fig. 2F), demonstrating a clear context-specific synthetic lethality. This is consistent with the established role of SOS1 and SOS2 as the primary RAS GEFs required for efficient GTP loading for downstream EGFR signaling(42). In contrast, oncogenic KRAS and BRAF are not fully dependent on SOS function, explaining the absence of a synthetic interaction in those genetic contexts. Prior studies have shown that loss of SOS1 or SOS2 impairs signaling in EGFR-mutant cells(43–46); our data extends these findings by demonstrating functional redundancy between SOS1 and SOS2 in EGFR-driven models.

Similarly, RAS paralogs KRAS and NRAS show no single knockout fitness defect in EGFR-dependent cells, but double knockouts indicate clear synthetic lethality in EGFR-dependent PC9 cells (Fig. 2G). This is similar to the KRAS-NRAS synthetic lethality we previously observed in BCR-ABL fusion K562 leukemia cells(35), but neither single nor double knockouts were lethal in MDA-MB-468 cells. This differential sensitivity may be explained by compensation from HRAS in MDA-MB-468 cells or may simply be a false negative from poor knockout efficiency. Neither single nor double knockout of KRAS and NRAS shows phenotype in BRAFmut cells, consistent with BRAF functioning downstream of RAS, while the severe double knockout phenotype in KRASmut cells is entirely explained by the KRAS single knockout (Fig. 2G), an example of mutation-driven epistasis. ERK genes MAPK1 and MAPK3, paralogs at the end of the MAP kinase cascade, show strong synthetic lethality across all eight cells (Fig. 2H).

Moving beyond paralogs, a summary view illustrates which genetic interactions are background-specific. Taking the Zgi score for each gene pair and performing a linear regression across the three genotypes identifies GAB1/GRB2 and SOS1/SOS2 as synthetic lethal in the EGFR background, consistent with these genes’ roles in the RTK signal transduction complex (Fig. 2, I and J). In contrast, PTPN11/RASA2 and MAPK1/3, while strong across all three backgrounds, show relative weakness (PTPN11/RASA2) and strength (KRAS/NRAS, MAPK1/3) in EGFR relative to the RAS/RAF mutants (Fig. 2, K to M).

Suppressor interactions are also evident. Knockout of the G-protein β-subunits GNB1 and GNB2 appears to suppress dependency on EGFR (Fig. 2, N to R), indicating the functional crosstalk between EGFR and GPCR. Prior studies have shown the transactivation of EGFR by GPCR(47), but the precise mechanism of this suppressor interaction remains unknown. In contrast, loss of PEA15 reduces the single-gene dependency on either MAPK1 or MAPK3 in BRAF-mutant cells (Fig. 2, O, S and T). PEA15 encodes a protein that sequesters activated MAP kinase protein in the cytoplasm, and BRAFV600E cells are generally associated with a strong preference for MAPK1 over MAPK3(12, 39, 48). Loss of PEA15 leads to increased nuclear translocation of MAP kinase protein(49–51), likely offsetting any loss of proliferation signaling by ERK in its transcriptional activation role when one copy is lost to genetic perturbation. Overall, this subnetwork shows both known and novel genetic interactions, and highlights the dominance of paralog synthetic lethality in genetic interaction networks.

sec.title: Integration across screens to identify weaker interactions
sec.p: To more confidently identify synthetic interactions with large effect sizes, we set thresholds for genetic interaction (Zgi < −2.5), double knockout phenotype (Zfc < −2), and delta log fold change, the genetic interaction score as measured only by the single and double knockout guide arrays (dLFC < −1) (Fig. 3A). We previously showed that using both genetic interaction and fold change thresholds was important for identifying high-quality paralog synthetic lethals(52). We find a median of 77 high-effect size (HE) interactions per screen across the eight high quality screens, with a strong relationship between screen quality and number of SL hits discovered (Spearman rho = −0.90, P=0.002; Fig. 3B).

These high effect size hits represent a very small fraction of the total number of gene pairs assayed in the RTK library (median 0.4% of tested pairs; Fig. 3B). We sought to integrate data across the eight screens to attempt to separate consistent but weaker interactions from background noise. Importantly, the Zgi score is normally distributed for each (Fig. 3C and figs, S4 to S6), providing a robust statistical foundation for our integrative approach. We calculated a normalized Z-score for each gene pair across all eight cell lines (hereafter normZ), which showed a much greater dynamic range, though still normally distributed around zero (Fig. 3D). Shuffling labels within each cell line and re-calculating the normZ score rescued the near-perfect normal distribution (Fig. 3E), indicating our null model is reasonable.

We converted normZ scores to one-sided P-values separately for both synthetic and suppressor interactions and applied a Benjamini & Hochberg adjustment to identify both positive and negative interactions at a 1% theoretical false discovery rate. We recovered 932 negative interactions at this threshold, while randomization by label shuffling data 1000x typically yielded less than 10 (Fig. 3, F and G). Mapping these interactions onto the hierarchical RTK network from Figure 1 identifies a dense network of genetic interactions in the ER-localized protein glycosylation pathway (Fig. 3H). Asparagine-linked glycosylation (ALG) occurs at the intersection of the two pathways constructing the glycan tree and cotranslationally translocating nascent peptide sequences at the rough ER. Glycan biosynthesis involves three phases, broadly defined by sequential activity of transferases of N-acetyl-glucosamine (GlcNAc), mannose, and glucose; the GlcNAc component was not included in this library. Cotranslational translocation occurs at the Sec61 translocation complex in cooperation with the signal sequence receptor complex. The oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) complex, which occurs as two isoforms with a shared OST4 subunit, is co-located with the Sec61 complex on the ER membrane and transfers the completed glycan onto the translocating peptide chain at specific asparagine residues(53, 54).

We identify strong evidence of consistent within- and between-pathway interactions, including synthetic lethality between the OST4 complex and the glucosyltransferase pathway, especially ALG5 and ALG6 (Fig. 3H), and between the subunits of the Sec61 translocon complex and the signal sequence receptor complex. OST4 is required for efficient N-glycosylation by stabilizing the native OST complexes(55). Depletion of OST4 will reduce but not eliminate OST complex function(56). ALG5/6 acts upstream in the synthesis of glucose-modified lipid-linked oligosaccharides: ALG5 catalyzes the formation of the donor-substrate dolichol phosphate-glucose, and ALG6 transfers the first glucose onto the growing oligosaccharide. Absence of this terminal glucose residue impairs glycan recognition and leads to reduced N-glycosylation(57). These observations provide a potential mechanism for the synthetic lethality we observe between OST4 and ALG5/ALG6. Similarly, SSR2/3 are components of the translocon-associated TRAP complex, which functions as a chaperone or facilitator to assist Sec61 translocon. SEC62 and SEC63 are core components of the Sec61 translocon channel complex, and when either is lost, cells become more dependent on TRAP to stabilize Sec61 and maintain minimal translocation activity(58). These identifications illustrate redundant functional relationships between non-paralogous genes. The two OST complex isoforms are distinguished by paralogs STT3A/B, which are strong synthetic lethals across all our screens, while the STT3A complex isoform shows positive interactions between its subunits OSTC-STT3A and OSTC-OST4. Paralogs SEC61A1/2 that encode the Sec61 channel are not in our RTK network but are strong synthetic lethals.

A brief list of the top normZ synthetic lethals (Fig. 3I) shows three interactions, STT3A/B, SEC63/SSR3, and ALG5/OST4, in this glycosylation subnetwork. Other top hits include the HDAC1/2 and CDK4/6 positive controls and known paralog synthetic lethals MAPK1/3, SOS1/2, and MAP2K1/2. Strong novel interactions are readily confirmed, with color competition assays with OST4 knockout paired with either ALG5 or ALG6 showing strong genetic interaction in both HT29 and PC9 cells (Fig. 3, J and K). These interactions are evident even after short incubations, consistent with high effect size and high penetrance.

Genes with positive knockout phenotypes may be enriched for false positives. Two of the high normZ interactions in Figure 3I, B3GALT6/RDH14 and RCE1/RDH14, appear to be evidence of systematic false positives using this approach. While the basic model of expected double knockout (DKO) fold change being the sum of single knockout (SKO) fold change is strongly supported by our regression model and the bulk of published research, it fails when SKO fold change is moderately positive. This may not be particularly rare, as we expect null-phenotype knockouts to be represented by fold changes normally distributed around zero. However, according to the additive (in log space) model, the expected DKO of two SKO > 0 is more positive, rather than closer to 0, so even a null DKO phenotype would result in a negative GI score. This is the case for the two reported RDH14 interactions, where all three involved genes have beta scores > 0, and double knockouts > 0 but less than the -- clearly false -- expectation from the sum of beta scores (fig. S7). This may be a systematic feature of double knockout screens analyzed by log fold change.

sec.title: Interactions maintained in physiologically relevant models
sec.p: A fundamental question about genetic screens in cancer cell lines is whether the genetic dependencies and interactions discovered in 2D culture hold any relevance in more physiologically relevant conditions. To test this, we constructed a small validation library for testing high-effect hits in different models grown under different conditions (Fig. 3L). The library probes all pairs of 29 target genes, primarily drawn from the genes shown in the subnetwork in Figure 3H. We screened the library in the B1003 patient-derived colorectal tumor cells in 2D culture and in mouse xenografts, in a patient-derived organoid model grown in 3D culture, and in HT29 cells grown in 2D and 3D cultures as well as in mouse xenografts. We found that the 2D cultures outperformed 3D and in vivo (Fig. 3, M and N; fig S8), but that the highest effect size hits were still detectable even using mouse xenograft models, with both HT29 and B1003 xenograft screens achieving ~50% recall of top hits at 25% FDR. Thus, robust hits in 2D models appear to be good predictors of genetic interactions in more physiologically relevant contexts.

Identifying clinically relevant contexts to exploit cellular genetic interactions can be challenging. In the most straightforward case, a synthetic lethal pair where one gene is commonly mutated, deleted, or silenced in tumors can lead to tumor-specific vulnerability to clinical targeting of the partner gene. This paradigm underlies the BRCA mutation/PARP inhibitor synergy first explored by Ashworth(59) and later expanded to include HR deficiency more broadly, including discovery of new DNA repair genes whose copy loss in specific tissues could be used to expand therapeutic options(60). Following this approach, we took our genes from the dense subnetwork in Figure 3H and looked for tumors across the TCGA PanCancer cohort with frequent deletions using cBioPortal(61). Surprisingly, we discovered that most of the genes were amplified, rather than deleted, and that co-amplification of multiple genes in the network was prevalent (fig. S9A). Narrowing our search to the 14 genes which showed minimal deletions (Fig. 3O), and including only tumors wherein at least 14% of samples showed amplification of one or more of our target genes (fig. S9B), we found a striking association between amplification of glycosylation genes and reduced overall cancer survival (Fig. 3P). Among the top four tumor types, uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma, soft tissue sarcoma, stomach adenocarcinoma, and hepatocellular carcinoma, median survival is reduced by half, from 91 months to 45, when amplification of glycosylation genes is present (HR 1.62; 95% CI 1.29–2.02; Logrank P-val 1.7×10−6). A similar hazard ratio is observed when considering the entire TCGA PanCancer cohort (Fig. 3Q), but disappears when these four tumors are removed.

sec.title: Genetic interactions in the DDR module
sec.p: We used the same analytical approach in the DDR sublibrary. Clustering cells by their response to knockout of TP53 and its regulators MDM2/MDM4 clearly separated TP53wt cells from TP53LOF cells (Fig. 4A). Cells with high microsatellite instability (LS180, HCT116) are characterized by high dependency on Werner helicase (WRN), which is coincident with TP53wt. We measured high-effect hits as with the RTK library and identified ~250 synthetic lethals per cell line (Fig. 4B), though without the same correlation with screen quality (Fig. 3B). In contrast, a similar analysis for suppressor interactions yielded a much smaller count (median 14 per cell line; Fig. 4C), with more than twice as many interactions per cell in TP53wt cells. Paralogs are again among the top common HE synthetic lethals, including iron sensors ACO1/IREB2 (Fig. 4, D and E) and ribosomal proteins (and possibly cryptic tumor suppressors) RPL22/RPL22L1 (Fig. 4, F and G). We compared mean Zgi scores in TP53LOF and TP53wt backgrounds to evaluate the overall abundance of P53-specific interactions and found several negative interactions that were considerably stronger in TP53LOF backgrounds. Interestingly, we observe the synthetic lethal interaction between base excision repair endonuclease APEX2 and two RNASEH2 complex subunits (Fig. 4, I and J), which has been reported and reconfirmed in the literature(63–65), to be comparatively weak in TP53wt backgrounds. In contrast, the sole TP53wt-specific interaction, RFC2/TP53 (Fig. 4K), may be another systematic false positive, as TP53 knockout shows positive Zfc in TP53wt backgrounds (Fig. 4L). TP53/RFC2 double knockout phenotype is consistent, however, independent of P53 state, and suggesting a dominant phenotype from RFC2 loss.

We integrated DDR hits across cell lines using the normalized Z score approach. As with the RTK library, the individual hits in DDR are normally distributed, and shuffled Z-scores give a near-perfect normal distribution, confirming the null model. We calculated enrichment of interactions within and between modules in the network (The DDR network is shown in fig. S1G) and found clear indications of module-specific interactions; a high-density subnetwork of modules is shown in Figure 4M. Interaction density is dominated by the RFC complex, with consistent interactions with LIG4/XRCC4 – an emergent module from the DDR coessentiality network – and with the CTF18 subcomplex, which interacts with RFC to facilitate PCNA loading for leading strand synthesis(66–68). A global view of between-complex synthetic interactions and within-module suppressor interactions is shown in Figure 4N (figs. S10 and S11).

Our DDR library is substantially smaller than the massive DDR genetic interaction study recently described by Fielden et al.(19), whose study had triple the genes (Fig. 4O) and ten times the gene pairs (Fig. 4P). Among the 3,741 gene pairs assayed by both teams, the intersection between our top normZ scores (theoretical FDR < 1%) and their top Gemini(26) scores was ~50% greater than random expectation (P-val 1.6×10−3, hypergeometric test; Fig. 4Q). Within the normZ hits, the distribution of high-effect hits was similar in the intersection and in the normZ-only hits (Fig. 4R), while the Fielden-only hits were almost never detected as high-effect hits in our screens. The FANCM/SMARCAL1 interaction characterized in the Fielden et al. study is among the strongest hits in our DDR analysis, being observed as a high-effect interaction in 4 of 8 screens. Interestingly, the strong APEX2/RNASEH2 interactions are not detected in the Fielden screen, which was conducted in TP53wt RPE-1 cells. Overall, while the concordance between the two screens is statistically significant, the large number of hits unique to each study is likely due to some combination of background-specific hits, the different perturbation modalities (CRISPRi vs CRISPRko) and analysis pipelines used, and a difficult-to-characterize false positive and especially false negative rate in CRISPR-mediated genetic interaction screens.

sec.title: Global characteristics of genetic interactions
sec.p: We attempted to discern global characteristics of high-effect genetic interactions by comparing the DDR and RTK screens. The DDR library yielded a substantially greater number of negative high-effect interactions per cell line (median 251 vs 77, Fig. 5A) but less than half the number of positive high-effect interactions (median 14 vs 34, Fig. 5B). The number of interactions per gene also differed widely. In the RTK module, most genes had no strong interaction, and the degree distribution of negative interactions was slightly greater than positives (Fig. 5C). In contrast, in the DDR gene set, nearly all genes had at least one high-effect negative interaction, and most had more than one (Fig. 5D). This is consistent with previous observations in yeast and human cells(2, 22) that genes which show some single knockout phenotype are generally more likely to have genetic interactions than genes which have no LOF fitness phenotype. In fact, within the RTK gene set, genes with a high-effect negative interaction tend to have more severe single knockout fitness phenotype than genes without (Fig. 5E). This is not seen in the DDR gene set, probably because most genes have an interaction (Fig. 5D), confounded by the fact that, overall, the DDR genes have a much more severe single knockout phenotype than the RTK genes. In contrast, within the DDR genes, genes with a positive interaction are less likely to have a single knockout phenotype (Fig. 5F), but this is not observed in RTK.

Looking more broadly at normZ interactions discovered by integrating signal across cell lines, we observe more DDR interactions (theoretical FDR < 1%), both positive and negative, than RTK interactions (Fig. 5G), and when correcting for the number of pairs tested, DDR interactions are observed at nearly twice the frequency (Fig. 5H). Both negative and positive RTK interactions are more common among genes with higher coessentiality metrics (Fig.5, I and J). Negative interactions between DDR genes are also correlated with coessentiality (Fig. 5K), but the relationship disappears for positive interactions (Fig. 5L).

Paralogs remain the dominant source of high-penetrance synthetic lethal interactions with large effect sizes. Paralogs are more than 14-fold enriched in RTK interactions and 6-fold enriched in DDR interactions (Fig. 5M). Paralog synthetic lethals consistently among the most common and most high-scoring high-effect interactions and, in turn, the strongest normZ interactions as well. Synthetic interactions are also enriched for protein-protein interactions in both RTK (2.9-fold) and DDR (1.7-fold; Fig. 5M) high-effect interactions, but suppressor interactions are not, somewhat surprising given the presence of within-module suppressor interactions (fig. S9).

While there are clearly a significant number of interactions in both the DDR and RTK networks, their abundance alone does not provide evidence for or against our predictive model of genetic interactions (Fig. 1, B to E). To estimate the background density of genetic interactions, we randomly selected 80 genes with no meaningful coessentiality and added three paralog pairs (six genes) and three tumor suppressor genes (TP53, PTEN, and NF2), for a total of 89 genes. We constructed a genetic interaction library targeting all pairs of these genes with three arrays targeting each gene pair and screened the resulting 12k library in three cell lines (Fig. 5N). We applied the GRAPE analytical pipeline and observed that, in all three screens, only the positive control paralogs met the threshold for high effect size hits (Fig. 5O). We relaxed the threshold to Zgi <-2, with no corresponding Zfc threshold, to enable comparison. Across each of the 8 screens performed with the RTK/DDR library, we observed enrichment of ~5-fold among RTK genes and ~16 fold for DDR genes (Fig. 5P). We performed a similar analysis using the normZ approach, calculating normZ for all combinations of three cell lines and comparing with the three-screen normZ calculated from the random library and observing enrichment of two- to eight-fold (Fig. 5Q). Overall, these results confirm that our network decomposition approach identifies modules that are highly enriched for genetic interactions.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Systematic mapping of genetic interactions in human cells has been limited by the immense combinatorial search space and the resource-intensive nature of multiplex perturbation screens. Here, we demonstrate that principles governing genetic interaction architecture in yeast, specifically, that functionally coherent modules are enriched for within-module interactions, can be used to prioritize regions of the human genome for combinatorial screening. By decomposing human co-essentiality networks into functional modules and selecting large gene sets with high internal functional coherence, we achieved 5- to 16-fold enrichment of genetic interactions relative to randomly selected gene pairs. This network-guided approach enables efficient discovery of synthetic lethal and suppressor interactions without exhaustive screening of all possible gene combinations.

Our screens uncovered hundreds of genetic interactions across the two functionally distinct modules. Within the RTK signaling network, we identified both universal interactions, such as the broadly penetrant MAPK1/MAPK3 and STT3A/STT3B synthetic lethalities, and context-specific vulnerabilities that depend on oncogenic background. The dense network of interactions within the ER-localized protein glycosylation machinery, connecting the oligosaccharyltransferase complex, glucosyltransferases, and the Sec61 translocon channel, represents a previously unappreciated hub of synthetic lethality with potential therapeutic implications. The observation that amplification of glycosylation pathway genes correlates with reduced patient survival across multiple tumor types suggests that these interactions may be clinically relevant, though the mechanistic basis for this association requires further investigation. Within the DDR module, we recovered known interactions such as FANCM/SMARCAL1, but the discovery that a commonly reported interaction like APEX2/RNASEH2 is substantially stronger in TP53-deficient backgrounds highlights the risk of generalizing interactions observed in small numbers of samples. Perhaps not surprisingly, paralogs emerged as the dominant source of high-penetrance synthetic lethal interactions with large effect sizes in both modules, consistent with the previously reported higher density of genetic interactions among paralogs.

A key finding is that genetic interactions discovered in standard 2D cell culture retain relevance in more physiologically complex models. Our validation experiments demonstrated that high-effect interactions identified in 2D screens are detectable in 3D organoid cultures and mouse xenografts, with recall of top hits even in a patient-derived tumor model screened in a challenging in vivo setting. This suggests that robust hits from 2D screening provide a reasonable starting point for cancer target discovery, though the reduced signal-to-noise in 3D and in vivo models underscores the importance of prioritizing interactions with large effect sizes for translational studies.

Despite the advances shown here, our approach is not without limitations. First, our module decomposition method relies on the completeness of the underlying co-essentiality network, which is itself derived from CRISPR screens in cancer cell lines and does not fully capture functional relationships relevant to normal tissues or specific tumor contexts(13). Second, our focus on genetic interaction screening within functionally coherent modules offers relatively high density of genetic interactions but necessarily limits recall of the true synthetic lethal network. Indeed, our analysis in yeast suggests 10% of all synthetic lethals can be identified by screening 1% of gene pairs, fruitful guidance for targeted experiments but leaving the bulk of synthetic lethals unassayed. Finally, in the absence of gold standards against which to measure the quality of these large-scale screens, the modest overlap between individual screens and with the independent Fielden et al. DDR screen, highlight the challenge of reproducibility in this field and suggest that both false positive and false negative rates remain significant. Nevertheless, the framework we establish here—network decomposition to identify interaction-dense modules, efficient In4mer-based combinatorial screening, and integration across cellular contexts, provides a scalable strategy for systematic genetic interaction mapping in human cells.

caption.title: Network-guided design of genetic interaction screens.
caption.p: (A) Schematic of goals. Combinatorial targeting of tumor-specific synthetic lethals is a goal for precision medicine. (B) Yeast genetic interaction networks of double knockouts of gene 1 (x-axis) and gene 2 (y-axis), where profile similarity of genetic interaction profiles indicates similar biological function, creating a functional interaction network. (C) Dissecting the functional network suggests that large modules (x-axis) with high functional coherence (y-axis) are highly enriched for genetic interactions (colorbar), providing a rubric for prioritizing genetic interaction screens. (D) CRISPR screens in cancer cell lines provide a similar insight into functional relationships between genes: correlated fitness profiles indicate functional similarity. (E) Decomposition of the human functional interaction network identifies large modules (x-axis) with high functional coherence (y-axis), that we hypothesize are enriched for genetic interactions. (F) The RTK module as constructed using our network decomposition approach whereby genes (black label) are progressively collapsed into modules. After the structure is learned, paralogs (blue label) are added to each module. Numbers on each module (purple) indicate number of genes. Moonlighters (yellow) are associated with two different modules. See Methods for details. (G) Design of Cas12a guide arrays targeting single and double gene knockouts, using In4mer constructs. (H) A single library targets all pairs of 199 RTK genes, all pairs of 167 DDR genes, and all individual 4,435 paralog pairs. 104 paralogs are duplicated in the RTK and DDR modules. (I-J) Kernel density estimates of guide arrays targeting control essential (red) and nonessential (blue) genes in a high-quality screen, PC9, and a lower quality screen, A549. (K) Separation of essentials and nonessentials was used to measure Cohen’s D for each cell line. (L) For each screen, fold changes across all targets were normalized to a Z-score by fitting the main peak of the fold change distribution to a gaussian. (M) Clustering of Zfc across 13 targets in the RTK/MAP kinase cascade clearly distinguishes BRAFmut, KRASmut, and EGFR-dependent cells.

caption.title: Global and background-specific genetic interactions.
caption.p: (A) the GRAPE algorithm learns regression coefficients that estimate single gene knockout phenotype (fold change), calculates an expected double knockout phenotype, measures the deviation from this phenotype, and then calculates a Z-score of the deviation. (B) Observed Zfc (y-axis) vs. Zfc predicted from single gene regression coefficients (x-axis). (C) Raw GI score is observed – expected, as a function of expected Zfc. A sliding window estimates local standard deviation (red) for calculating Z-score of GI. (D) Z-score of GI (y-axis) vs. predicted Zfc (x-axis). Negative GI are synthetic lethal; labeled pairs are synthetic lethal paralog pairs. (E) As a sanity check, observed single KO from the guide arrays targeting a single gene are plotted against single gene beta coefficients from GRAPE. Outliers represent inconsistency and are flagged or removed from downstream analysis. (F) Zfc for the SOS1_SOS2 paralog pair across all 8 high quality screens. SOS1: Zfc of all genes paired with SOS1. SOS2: Zfc of all genes paired with SOS2. Black segment indicates expected single knockout Zfc from GRAPE. (G-H) Zfc plots for background-specific KRAS_NRAS and global MAPK1_MAPK3 synthetic lethality. (I-M) Negative/synthetic Zgi scores for labeled gene pairs in each cell line, separated by oncogenic driver (red, EGFR; blue, BRAF; purple, KRAS). (N) Suppressor interaction between EGFR and GNB2. (O) RTK and MAP kinase signaling network, showing strong synthetic and suppressor interactions. (P-T) Positive/suppressor Zgi scores for labeled gene pairs in each cell line, separated by oncogenic driver.

caption.title: Integrative analysis of interactions.
caption.p: (A) Distributions of Zgi, Zfc, and dLFC, showing thresholds for calling high-effect-size (HE) synthetic interactions: Zgi < −2.5, Zfc < −2, and dLFC < −1. (B) Number (left axis) and frequency (right axis) of HE interactions across eight high-quality screens. Cell lines are sorted from best to worst quality score; Spearman correlation between screen quality and number of HE hits shown in inset. (C) Q-Q plot of Zgi for a single screen. (D) Q-Q plot of normZ scores across all 8 screens, with higher dynamic range than single-screen distributions. (E) Q-Q plot of normZ scores of label-shuffled Zgi across 8 screens shows expected normal distribution. (F) Number of synthetic lethal hits from normZ randomization across 1,000 iterations (blue), vs. number observed in data (red, n=932). (G) Average left-tailed P-value distribution of normZ randomization (blue) vs. observed in data (orange). (H) Protein glycosylation subnetwork; edges indicate normZ score. (I) Top normZ synthetic lethal hits. (J-K) Color competition assays for two novel interactions, ALG5_OST4 and ALG6_OST4, in HT29 (J) and PC9 (K) cells. (L) A 1.5k validation library for testing whether interactions in 2D are also present in more complex models. Created with Biorender.com. (M) Precision-recall plots for six validation library screens. (N) Recall at 25% FDR (75% precision) for each of the six validation screens confirms interactions with high effect size are present in 3D and in vivo models. (O) Oncoprint showing copy amplification of genes in the glycosylation GI network. Data from TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas; graphic from cBioPortal. (P) Across the top four tumor types, copy amplification in one or more of the glycosylation network genes is associated with severely reduced survival (median 45 vs 91 months). (Q) Hazard ratios for the top four tumor types individually and collectively, and across all Pan-Cancer Atlas tissues. **, P-val < 0.01.

caption.title: Interactions in the DDR network.
caption.p: (A) Zfc in TP53-associated genes segregates cells into TP53LOF and TP53wt groups. WRN-dependent MSI-high cells are confounded with TP53wt. (B-C) Number (left y-axis) and frequency (right) of high-effect DDR SL (B) and suppressor (C) interactions. (D) Zfc of highly penetrant ACO1_IREB2 paralog synthetic lethals, and (E) corresponding Zgi plots separated by TP53 status. (F-G), same for paralogs RPL22-RPL22L1. (H) Mean Zgi in TP53LOF vs TP53wt cells to identify background-specific interactions. (I-J) Zgi plots of APEX2 vs RNASEH2 complex subunits show stronger interactions in TP53LOF cells. (K) RFC2/TP53 interaction appears to be TP53-wtspecific, but (L) Zfc data shows consistent double knockout phenotype. (M) Network of genetic interactions between modules identified in the network decomposition; color as in Figure 3H. (N) Enrichment of within-module epistatic (positive) and between-module synthetic (negative) interactions as measured by permutation analysis. (O) Comparison of DDR genes targeted in this study vs. Fielden et al. (P) Comparison of gene pairs targeted in this study vs. Fielden et al. Inset, distribution of hits among 3,741 gene pairs assayed by both, using normZ integrative scores. (Q) Each hit in the intersection was measured for how many cell lines in which it was identified as a high-effect size interaction. (R) NormZ scores (x-axis) vs. Gemini scores from Fielden et al. for 3,741 gene pairs. Black, interactions characterized in Fielden et al.

caption.title: Characteristics of genetic interactions.
caption.p: (A) Number of high-effect SL hits in RTK vs DDR modules. Each point is one cell line. (B) Number of high-effect suppressor hits. (C) Histogram of degree distribution of negative and positive GI in the RTK module. Most genes show no interactions. Error bars are stdev across 8 cell lines. (D) Histogram of degree distribution of negative and positive GI in the DDR module. In contrast with RTK, nearly every DDR gene has at least one high-effect SL interaction. (E) Kernel density estimate of single gene knockout phenotype (x-axis) for each gene in the cell line where it has an HE SL interaction (orange), vs. all genes in all cells (gray) in RTK module. Genes with fitness phenotype show more negative GI. (F) Kernel density estimate of single gene knockout phenotype (x-axis) for each gene in the cell line where it has an HE positive genetic interaction (blue), vs. all genes in all cells (gray) in DDR module. Most genes show single knockout fitness phenotype; genes with positive GI do not. (G-H) Number (G) and frequency (H) of synthetic and suppressor interactions by normZ in RTK (purple) and DDR (green) networks. (I-K) Correlation between pairwise gene coessentiality and frequency of SL in RTK (I) and DDR (K). (J-L) Correlation between pairwise gene coessentiality and frequency of suppressor interactions in RTK (J) and DDR (L). (M) Enrichment for protein-protein interactions and paralogs among synthetic and suppressor interactions in RTK and DDR. (N) Random library to estimate background frequency of genetic interactions. 12k library screened in HT29, PC9 and MDA-MB-468 cell lines. (O) GRAPE analysis of random library in HT29 cells yields only 3 hits at adjusted P-value < 0.01; all are positive control paralog synthetic lethals. (P) Enrichment of high-effect synthetic lethals in RTK and DDR networks relative to random library. (Q) Enrichment of normZ synthetic lethals in RTK and DDR networks relative to random library. Violin plots represent distribution across all permutations of 3 DDR screens, to facilitate comparison with 3 random library screens.
